entries.name: House Montrose
entries.conf: exact — GPS extracted from site-photo EXIF data
entries.citation:
In Oranjezicht, Cape Town, KLG Architects have radically transformed an existing house from a dwelling of rooms into a realm of spatial experiences.

Exploring the constraint of a typical narrow sloping site, the designers have reimagined the existing and conceived a contemporary dwelling through an exceptionally well crafted building. Entering on the upper level one is confronted by a small glazed courtyard space where a portion of the raw site is maintained within its transparent enclosure — providing a reference point within the radically reconfigured open plan and thereby establishing relations between the house, nature and the city and the encompassing Table Bay beyond.

On the south the living areas ceiling is significantly manipulated and raised to frame the rear outside whilst extending across to encompass Table Mountain into and across the living space and a hidden study area above. The sensation is one of reconnection between the city's primary natural elements — mountain and sea.

The limited material palette reflects on early Cape Modernism, predominantly through the disciplined use of white painted masonry enclosure, complemented by an evolving sensibility with timberwork. The work is clearly recognisable as a design by KLG, whose projects have over recent years become consistently rewarded in recognition of a continually evolving design language.

entries.name: Mostert's Mill
entries.citation:
Immaculate restoration has returned the mill, ravaged by a fire in 2021, to full working order, transforming it from a static reminder of the past into a living demonstration of heritage in motion. The project carefully balanced preservation with reconstruction, conserving all surviving original components while faithfully recreating lost elements, including the swivelling roof cap, sails, and intricate internal mechanisms.

The educational aspect is particularly laudable. Visitors can once again observe the mill's operation and gain insight into the craftsmanship, engineering, and historical context that define its significance. By prioritising accuracy and functionality, the restoration provides a rare, tangible learning experience that bridges past and present.

Ultimately, this project stands as a celebration of technology — both historic and modern. The result is a vibrant, working monument that honours its origins while inspiring future generations through its renewed purpose and accessibility.

entries.name: Redhill Early Learning Centre
entries.citation:
The architect introduces a "new complex world" into the space of the existing school, rendering both spaces unrecognisable to each other. The new spatial language is generated by the pedagogy of the Reggio Emilia schools in Italy. The exaggerated entrance is cleverly a "magical" threshold that dissolves reality.

This new spatiality, free from conventional geometries and conventional architectural languages, engages the imagination, provoking spatial exploration by the children — enhancing physical and mental development by enriching perception, building physical prowess, and encountering different levels of illumination and scale.

The colours are unexpected, nurturing pastel tones. Imposing high walls are dissolved using mosaics to simultaneously attenuate the ear and the eye. The floor is a warm, moulded ground plane and the datum of the child.

entries.name: House Hill
entries.citation:
House Hill-Venter is a re-innovation of an existing house on a standard Parkhurst allotment by Monograph Architects, for clients with a collection of modernist furniture and an evolved appreciation for the critical role that imagination plays in architectural design.

The entry façade appears as a regular residence in a typical Parkhurst street — optics are the outcome, not the generator, of this architecture. The ground plan has been radically reconfigured to establish a complex set of new relationships between site and natural/built, public/private, indoor/outdoor, creatively responding to the clients' need to accommodate their furniture collection, paintings and other artefacts.

A series of living areas flow together permitting informal everyday living, dining and entertaining, culminating in an external covered outdoor courtyard and a raised external dining platform. Green lightwells across the length of the building allow light to penetrate, altering experience across the highveld's seasonal climate.

This project is recognised for its ability to respond to client requirements with both integrity and imagination in transforming a regular suburban house into a veritable backdrop for dwelling in comfort.

entries.name: New Highveld House
entries.citation:
The materiality, geometries, and colours of this house dance in the sunshine. The Highveld House sits beautifully on a north-facing incline in Abbotsford, Johannesburg. Fluid space generated by exacting geometries along the slope ties together everyday and celebratory spaces both inside and outside this house.

Ribbons of space bathed in the colour of the sun erase traditional hierarchies of spaces in the home. Curving geometries extend space, creating contemplative thresholds, following inclines, arriving at exhibition walls and cave-like spaces. A white disc placed in the centre of ceiling planes gives the illusion of a series of domes floating above.

Strength of concrete block, plasticity of rammed earth, and delicate glazed steel planes receive an effortless ensemble of surreal, comforting waves of substance — all equivalent, all celebrated, both in summer and in winter.

entries.name: Upside Down House
entries.citation:
The Upside Down House, located in a residential golf estate in Kempton Park, is a masterfully crafted and conceptualised double-storey luxury home — a bold and sculptural piece of architectural work that rigorously integrates itself into the landscape, which belies its size. The name derives from its programme, with the primary living areas, including the master bedroom, on the upper level, taking advantage of views north towards the golf course.

The primary façade element constitutes a wrap-around screen of bronze-coloured aluminium fins that define the bold architectural character of the upper floor, juxtaposed against a well-detailed, executed concrete wall that grounds the composition — poetically an ode to the client's hobbies of woodwork and welding.

The home is entered from a centrally located courtyard introducing the two primary elements defining its character: the solid, deliberately heavy concrete base and the permeable screen above. Multiple moments of delight and surprise exude the character of this home, from the cavernous double-volume man-cave showcasing the client's classic cars, to the external staircase and hidden pool.

entries.name: Fluid Spaces
entries.citation:
This newbuild house, located within the Elaleni Coastal Forest Estate north of Durban, is sited on a small, irregular, triangular remainder allotment within a gated community. The architectural drawings reveal an exceptionally well-considered intervention within these strict limitations.

Working within a theme of "fluid spaces," the spatial configuration and dispersal of public and private functions afford an engaging place for dwelling in comfort. Solid enclosed space at the extremities anchors the intervention, whilst large openings establish spatial extension up to the perimeter, blurring the boundary between interior and exterior — in a sense, cleverly overwriting the building setbacks.

The outcome is reflective of exceptional design skill across the entire spectrum of architectural intervention, transforming the limitations of the site into spatial opportunities through consistent design innovation.

entries.name: Khanyisa
entries.citation:
Merging with the landscape — a challenge well met — this project responds deftly to its pivotal position on campus, shaping a building that is as much a pathway as a destination. Conceived to accommodate movement rather than simply arrival, it breaks down scale into a series of smaller, inhabitable zones that support both structured learning and the informal interactions that enrich daily school life.

Bold and confident, the architecture is defined by a striking roof form that anchors the building within its setting while signalling its presence at this key intersection. The design is culturally inclusive, demonstrating clear respect for the existing ethos of St Mary's, where holistic learning underpins every spatial decision. Areas for gathering, pausing and quiet reflection are carefully integrated to encourage curiosity, conversation, and moments of stillness beyond the classroom.

A robust, almost masculine detailing elevates otherwise mundane elements, lending the building a sense of engagement and tactile richness.

entries.name: Unbound
entries.citation:
Site has been exceedingly well used on this modestly sized home, located in a valley of an estate in Dullstroom, in a contemporary response to the farm-vernacular building guidelines of the estate. The stoep, low garden walls and detached-dwelling typology synonymous with the vernacular have been meticulously deconstructed to produce an architectural idiom that is highly sophisticated but very familiar.

Approaching the dwelling from the north and entering through a cascading landscaped courtyard, loosely contained by an aggregation of four buildings housing the homestead's programme, the spatial composition is diverse and fluid, with each building bearing complementary but differing visual and spatial characteristics.

Choice and composition of materiality is laudable, contributing productively to the landscaping within the property and beyond. Secondary elements — pergolas, clerestory glazing, steel rods demarcating site edges and thresholds — are articulately integrated into the well-conceived whole. This project robustly elevates traditional building elements like stone walls and corrugated roof sheeting to achieve an elegant, refined and restrained final product.

entries.name: Racquets Centre
entries.citation:
This project on a well-established sports club includes a new pavilion, six new padel courts and four additional tennis courts, with the pavilion housing changeroom facilities, a bar, pizza kitchen and upper terrace.

The project's success emanates from the architect's great respect for place — referencing the existing clubhouse structure as the datum point, the new pavilion finds the most optimised location on the sloping site, establishing and optimising the relationship of the built form with the natural landscape.

The single-storey pavilion is set into the landscape and slightly elevated on a podium, providing terraced seating while reinforcing the building's character. The roof terrace becomes a place for mingling or a spectator's vantage point over the padel courts, seamlessly integrating with the mini covered seating servicing the tennis courts on a different level of the site.

The faithful commitment to integrating landscape and topography with built form completes and complements this extensive intervention, rendering a very positive and elegantly timeless addition to place.

entries.name: Link Building
entries.loc: University of the Witwatersrand, East Campus, Braamfontein, Johannesburg
entries.arch: Lemon Pebble Architects + Urban Designers & SRS Architects

entries.name: The Barracks
entries.eng: Henry Fagan Consulting Engineers and Mericon
entries.citation:
This project renovates, repurposes and extends a historic 18th-century warehouse, which started life as a wine storage facility with a healthy historic relationship to the neighbouring Lutheran Church. It is a positive contribution to Cape Town's central business district — a triumphant example of a symbiotic and sympathetic conservation and contemporary adaptive-reuse scheme.

Laudable efforts to respect the historic skyline of the Lutheran Church have shaped the contemporary upper building's tectonic form. The new building is designed to be distinct from the historic building in materiality, form and tectonics, while establishing a common rhythm in the repetitive solid-and-void relationship of the façade.

Key positive attributes stem from the faithful restoration of the historic warehouse, which prompted the addition of a new multistorey built form above it — an inventive and innovative construction method that optimises the developmental yield of the site while ensuring structural independence between old and new. Upcycling of timber structural elements into ceiling panels, furniture and fixings is commendable, and the lift lobbies have become mini exhibition spaces of the architect's own research.

entries.name: House Vanayagar
entries.citation:
This home, designed by an architect for himself and his family, invites you to quieten your thoughts and be reflective, from approach to arrival. Upon entering, the phenomenological experience is heightened by the innovative placement of north-facing fenestration and a carved-out, multi-volume atrium and living rooms, translating the home's vantage point high on the ridge in the Berea suburb of Durban.

The commitment to sustainable practice is to be lauded — manifest in the upcycling and reuse of clay brick that defines the primary living areas' spatial character, and a chimney-stack effect through the double-volume entrance hall. The bare recycled brick walls bring warmth into the space and render it a place of memory, complemented by timber flooring and slate tiling applied coherently throughout, reinforcing restraint and quiet elegance.

The vantage point affords the primary living areas and master bedroom generous views towards the ocean and gardens. Roof-mounted solar panels and water harvesting round out the home's commitment to sustainable, realistic home ownership.
